content:
Mio looked away too quickly.

“They’re going to try to work out what I am,” she said.

Touma had been looking at her face. Now he wasn’t sure where to look.

“They don’t have to know.”

“That isn’t the same as not deciding.” She folded her arms. “People love deciding. Saves them the trouble of actually looking.”

“We could keep you out of public until—”

“Until I’m normal?”

“That wasn’t what I meant.”

“Then try phrasing it like you don’t want my nervous system removed.”

From beside the door, Nico made a small, unhappy sound.

“I’ll be in the hall.”

He stepped out, leaving the door partly open. Touma could still see his shoulder through the gap. It was a decent attempt at giving them privacy, considering the room wasn’t built for it and Nico clearly wasn’t built for this.

Without him in it, the room seemed smaller.

Touma gestured toward the chair by the desk. “Do you want to sit down?”

“Why? Am I flickering?”

“No. I just thought you might want to sit.”

“You’re looking at me like a haunted projector.”

“I don’t know what expression I’m supposed to have.”

“Try one you’d use for a person.”

That hurt enough that he knew not to defend himself.

He sat on the edge of the futon. After a moment, Mio pulled out the chair and lowered herself onto it.

The chair squeaked.

Touma let out a breath.

It was such an ordinary noise. Cheap furniture complaining about weight. Nothing had passed through anything else. The seat held her; the legs stayed on the floor. For reasons he couldn’t have explained without making everything worse, that felt enormous.

“Don’t make that face,” she said.

“What face?”

“The one where you’re grateful the furniture hasn’t rejected me.”

He looked down at his hands.

“Sorry.”

The air conditioner had gone quiet. With nothing filling the space between their jokes, he could hear how hard they were both working.

He had thought she looked embarrassed. Maybe that was simply what fear looked like when it had a face and was trying not to show itself.

“Can you eat?” he asked.

Mio stared at him.

He winced. “That sounded less strange before I said it.”

“Did it?”

“Not much.”

She looked toward the desk. “I don’t know.”

He had wanted to offer something useful. Food. Water. A place to sit. Things a person could give another person without needing to understand what had happened to them.

But even the easy questions weren’t easy. She had a body in front of him, and he didn’t know what that meant for her. Whether she could get hungry. Whether sitting helped. Whether any of this hurt.

Her hand rested near the edge of the desk.

He wanted to take it.

The impulse was so immediate that he had already moved before he stopped himself. He settled his hand against his own knee instead.

Mio noticed.

“You were going to ask something.”

In the hallway, Nico shifted.

“I’m just going to—”

“Wait,” Touma said.

Nico stopped. Touma looked at him, then at Mio. There was nothing Nico could solve by staying, and keeping him there just because Touma was frightened seemed unfair to all three of them.

“Sorry. Never mind.”

Nico nodded without looking directly at either of them. His footsteps moved away.

Touma turned back to Mio.

“I was going to ask if it hurt.”

For a moment, the room did something wrong.

The edge of the desk seemed to slip sideways without moving. Mio’s outline failed to meet the chair behind her, then fitted against it again. Touma blinked, but the sensation remained: something had nearly lost its place.

Mio held very still.

“It’s worse when I try too hard,” she said.

“To do what?”

“Hold a shape that makes sense.”

Her finger twitched against the desk.

He made himself keep looking at her face.

“Okay,” he said. “Then we should have some ground rules.”

“Oh, good. Terms of service.”

“No surprise touching.”

Her expression changed a little.

“Either of us,” he added.

“Fine.”

“And tell me if something hurts.”

“Touma.”

“Or if something feels wrong. You don’t have to explain it first.”

“I don’t want to be a problem.”

He rubbed his palms against his knees. “People are problems.”

“Beautifully handled.”

“I mean people need things. They get hurt. They don’t always know what to do. That doesn’t mean they’re doing something wrong by being there.”

She watched him with an attention that made it difficult to keep talking.

“If you tell me something’s wrong, I’ll listen,” he said.

“Even if you can’t see it?”

“Yes.”

“Even if everything else says I’m fine?”

“Yes.”

He wanted to add something reassuring. A promise large enough to make her stop looking as though the answer might be taken away.

Instead, he left it there.

Mio glanced down at his hand on his knee, then back up.

“All right,” she said quietly.

It wasn’t trust. Not yet. But he thought she was beginning to want to believe him.

The door opened.

A support technician leaned into the room, already speaking.

“Sorry, Nico said the—”

He stopped when he saw Mio.

Touma watched surprise spread across his face. Not ordinary surprise at finding someone in a bedroom. Something brighter and worse: the look of a man who had stumbled onto a miracle and was already imagining telling someone else.

“Who’s that?”

Mio went perfectly still.

Touma stood too fast. The futon shifted behind his legs.

“None of your business.”

He heard how sharp it sounded. He also heard what it gave away.

The technician’s eyes moved from Mio to him, then back again. Curiosity changed into the beginnings of a story.

Touma felt embarrassment and fear arrive together. Whatever he said now would become part of it. The chair, the bedroom, his own stupid defensive voice—details someone could repeat, arrange, laugh over.

“Leave,” he said.

“I was only—”

“Please.”

The technician backed out. Touma shut the door.

For a moment, he kept his hand on the knob.

“That was public,” Mio said.

He turned.

She was still sitting exactly as she had been when the door opened.

“One person,” he said, and regretted it immediately.

“One person who can talk.”

“I know.”

“I was hoping for a more dramatic reveal. Better lighting. Maybe an introduction.”

Her voice was steady enough to make him worry.

He could still see the technician’s expression. There were too many eyes in the safehouse, too many doorways. By the time they decided what to say, someone else might already have said it for them.

“What do we do if people start asking?” she said.

“We lie.”

Mio looked at him.

“That’s your plan?”

“It’s the part I have so far.”

She made a small sound of disgust, but there was something almost affectionate in it. Almost.

Then she straightened.

“If I’m going to be seen, I refuse to be seen as a mistake.”

Touma didn’t answer immediately.

She wasn’t asking him to make her feel better. She was telling him what she would not let other people turn her into. Not an error they had caught. Not a symptom. Not something whose visibility was itself proof that it ought to be corrected.

“You’re not a mistake,” he said.

The words came out without any protection around them.

Mio looked at him, and he felt the danger of having said something sincerely enough that neither of them could pretend it was a joke.

Then she gave a small, shaky laugh.

It didn’t make her less frightened. He could still see that in the way she held her hands.

But for one second, the room was bearable.

A soft scraping came from outside it.

Touma looked toward the door.

Not footsteps. Not the handle.

The sound came again, farther along the wall: a slow, faint drag, like a fingertip being drawn across the other side.

Mio’s eyes followed his.

There was no visible movement in the plaster. Still, Touma had the awful impression of pressure gathering behind it, something pressing close without yet pushing through.

His limiter pulsed cold.

Not the familiar restraint. A warning.

He stayed between Mio and the door, though he had no idea whether that meant anything now.

“Touma,” she said.

He didn’t look away from the wall.

“Don’t let the system decide what I am.”

The plaster seemed to hold the silence against them.

Then the wall answered with a deeper scrape, as though something had heard her and leaned closer.
